SBOM DIFF CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

What changed between two SBOMs?

A CycloneDX or SPDX SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) from syft, docker sbom, trivy, or cdxgen records every package in a build. Paste the SBOM from before and after a change and this page reports exactly which packages were added, removed, or changed version — nothing else, and nothing about vulnerabilities or licenses.

Nothing is uploaded. Both files you paste are read in this browser and never leave your device, and this tool makes no network calls of its own.

1. Paste both SBOM documents

CycloneDX and SPDX JSON are both understood, and you can mix formats (one of each) — only each package's name and version are compared.

Paste a before and after SBOM above and click Diff.

Findings

ChangePackageBeforeAfter

Prefer a CLI, or want this in your own CI?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

python3 sbom_diff.py old.json new.json                  # human-readable
python3 sbom_diff.py old.json new.json --format json     # machine-readable
python3 sbom_diff.py old.json new.json --fail-on-change  # exit 2 if anything differs

Get sbom_diff.py from the repo — stdlib only, nothing to install, no network calls. Wire --fail-on-change into your own CI to catch an unexpected dependency drift before it merges.

Common questions

Why not just run diff on the two SBOM files?

Both CycloneDX and SPDX documents carry a serial number, a generation timestamp, and tool metadata that differ on every single run even when the package list is byte-for-byte identical. A line-based diff shows all of that noise before it shows you the one package that actually changed. This tool reads only the package name and version from each document and ignores everything else, so the output is the change itself, not the noise around it.

Does this tell me if a new or updated package is vulnerable?

No. This is a structural comparison only — it reports that a package is new, gone, or at a different version, and nothing about whether any version is safe, vulnerable, or appropriately licensed. It makes no network calls of any kind, so it never queries a vulnerability database on your behalf.

Does it upload my SBOM anywhere?

No. Both files you paste are read in this browser and never leave your device. An SBOM can reveal your entire internal dependency tree, including proprietary or unreleased component names, so this page makes no network requests of its own — pasting is the only way it sees anything.

What if the two files are in different formats — one CycloneDX, one SPDX?

That still works. Only each package's name and version are compared, and both formats expose those two fields, so a CycloneDX document can be diffed against an SPDX document from an earlier build with no conversion step.

What about a package that appears twice with different versions in the same build?

Handled directly: packages are matched by name, and the set of versions recorded under that name is compared rather than assuming exactly one. A monorepo pulling in two versions of the same library through different paths is reported as a version gained or lost, not silently collapsed to one or crashed on.

More: how this compares to diffing the raw SBOM JSON files by hand, and how this compares to the official cyclonedx-cli's diff command. If one small version bump produced a report full of changes, see why bumping one package can show up as dozens of changes.

Checking one build's manifest rather than diffing two: Docker Base Image Pin Check asks whether a Dockerfile's base image is pinned to a content digest, and License Drift Check diffs a raw npm/pip/cargo/go dependency tree's declared licenses between two snapshots rather than a standardized SBOM document — three different slices of the same "what does this build actually contain, and did it change" question.

Diffing an API contract instead of a build artifact: OpenAPI Breaking Change Check compares two OpenAPI 3.x documents and classifies each difference as breaking or not, for the same "did this change and does it matter" question applied to a REST API version instead of a dependency inventory.

Preparing for a security audit rather than diffing a build: SOC 2 Readiness Checker scores your controls against what auditors test and ranks the gaps by effort.

vs-cyclonedx-cli-diff.html.text:
← SBOM Diff Check

SBOM Diff Check vs. cyclonedx-cli diff

cyclonedx-cli is the official CycloneDX project's command-line tool, and its diff subcommand compares two CycloneDX documents. It is a real, maintained tool for a real slice of this job -- and it only reads CycloneDX, needs an install, and needs one extra flag before it lists which packages actually changed. This page reads CycloneDX or SPDX, mixed formats included, with nothing to install and nothing to remember.

What each tool is for

cyclonedx-cli (github.com/CycloneDX/cyclonedx-cli) is an Apache-2.0 licensed binary maintained under OWASP CycloneDX, installed with brew install cyclonedx/cyclonedx/cyclonedx-cli, the cyclonedx/cyclonedx-cli Docker image, or a release download for your platform. Its diff subcommand, per its own documented options, takes <from-file> <to-file> with --from-format/--to-format of autodetect, json, protobuf, or xml -- CycloneDX's own formats, not SPDX -- and needs the --component-versions flag to report which component versions were added, removed, or modified; without it you get a different, lower-level document diff. It also carries convert, merge, and validate subcommands this page has no equivalent of, because those are CycloneDX document operations rather than a before/after package comparison.

This tool reads only each component's name and version, from CycloneDX or SPDX JSON -- including one of each, no conversion step -- and always reports the added, removed, and version-changed packages, in your browser, with nothing to install and no flag to get right.

Where to answer each question.
QuestionWhere to answer it
Both my SBOMs are CycloneDX, and this needs to run inside a pipeline that already calls cyclonedx-cli for other operations.cyclonedx-cli diff --component-versions -- one more subcommand on a binary you already have installed.
One of my two files is SPDX, or came from a tool that emits SPDX by default.This page -- cyclonedx-cli diff does not accept SPDX input; you would need to convert first.
I want a quick answer with nothing to install, from a shared link or a support ticket.This page -- paste both files, get the list, nothing to set up.
I want CycloneDX-native operations beyond diffing -- convert, merge, validate a document against the spec.cyclonedx-cli -- this page does exactly one thing and has no equivalent for the rest.
Is anything I paste or pass uploaded anywhere?Neither tool uploads anything on its own -- this page reads both files in your browser and makes no network call of its own; cyclonedx-cli runs locally as a CLI.

The two are complementary rather than competing: a CycloneDX-only pipeline that already shells out to cyclonedx-cli loses nothing by keeping it for the diff step too. This page exists for the case it does not cover well -- SPDX input, or no CLI install at all.

Run the free SBOM diff

Common questions

Should I use this page or cyclonedx-cli's diff command?

Depends what you are diffing and where. cyclonedx-cli is the official CycloneDX project's command-line tool (Apache-2.0, maintained under OWASP CycloneDX), installed via Homebrew, a Docker image, or a downloaded release binary, and its diff subcommand compares two CycloneDX documents in JSON, XML, or protobuf. If both of your SBOMs are already CycloneDX and you want the comparison wired into a pipeline that already runs the CLI for other CycloneDX operations (convert, merge, validate), use cyclonedx-cli. If one of your two files is SPDX -- or you just want a quick answer with nothing to install -- this page reads CycloneDX or SPDX directly, including one of each, entirely in your browser.

Does cyclonedx-cli's diff command read SPDX SBOMs?

Not directly. Per its own documented options, diff accepts --from-format and --to-format values of autodetect, json, protobuf, or xml -- there is no spdxjson option there, unlike cyclonedx-cli's separate convert command, which does read SPDX JSON. Comparing an SPDX build against a CycloneDX build with cyclonedx-cli means converting the SPDX file to CycloneDX first as an extra step. This page compares CycloneDX and SPDX directly, in any combination, with no conversion.

Do I need to install anything to run cyclonedx-cli's diff command?

Yes. cyclonedx-cli is a standalone binary you get via brew install cyclonedx/cyclonedx/cyclonedx-cli, a Docker image (cyclonedx/cyclonedx-cli), or a release download for your platform -- there is no browser version. That is a reasonable cost for a tool meant to live in CI. This page needs nothing installed: paste both files and read the result in the same tab, or use the matching zero-dependency Python CLI linked from the tool page if you want the same logic in your own pipeline.

Does cyclonedx-cli diff list added, removed, and changed packages by default?

Only with a flag. Per its documented options, the base diff output compares the two documents; getting a components-level report of what was added, removed, or modified needs the --component-versions flag on the same invocation. Skip it and you get a lower-level document diff instead of the added/removed/changed list most people are actually asking for. This page always shows that list -- there is no equivalent flag to remember.

Is this page affiliated with CycloneDX, OWASP, or the cyclonedx-cli maintainers?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by CycloneDX, the OWASP Foundation, or the cyclonedx-cli maintainers. CycloneDX and cyclonedx-cli are named here only to describe what this checker is and is not, using facts drawn from the cyclonedx-cli project's own public documentation and source repository at github.com/CycloneDX/cyclonedx-cli.

vs-diffing-the-raw-json-files.html.text:
← back to the tool

This tool vs. diffing the raw SBOM JSON files by hand

The obvious first move when you want to know what changed between two SBOMs is diff old.json new.json, or pasting both into a generic JSON-diff tool. Both are close to useless for this specific question, and the reason is structural rather than a quality problem with either approach: a SBOM document carries metadata that changes on every generation run, and that metadata buries the one thing you actually asked about.

What each one is for

A raw diff or generic JSON-diff tool is correct and complete for comparing two JSON documents field-for-field. Its limit here is structural: a CycloneDX or SPDX document embeds a serial number, a generation timestamp, and the generating tool's own version string, and every one of those differs between two runs even when the package list is identical. On a real SBOM with hundreds of components, that metadata noise arrives before the one line you actually care about.

This tool reads only each component's name and version from both documents — CycloneDX or SPDX, and the two can even be mixed — and reports exactly which packages were added, removed, or changed version. It ignores every field a raw diff would show you that has nothing to do with what the build actually contains.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Did any package get added, removed, or bumped between two builds?This tool's added / removed / version-changed lists.
Is a required SBOM field present and correctly formatted on every component?Neither tool answers this — that is document validation, not change detection.
Can I compare a CycloneDX build against an SPDX build from before a tooling switch?This tool. Only name and version are compared, and both formats expose them.
Is an added or updated package actually safe to ship?Neither tool can answer this — both are structural comparisons with no vulnerability or license data.
Is anything I paste uploaded anywhere?No, for this tool — everything runs in your browser. A generic online JSON-diff tool may log or cache what you paste; check its own policy before pasting a full dependency inventory into one.

Common questions

What does a plain diff of two SBOM files actually show me?

Mostly noise. A CycloneDX or SPDX document embeds a serial number, a generation timestamp, and the generating tool's own version, and every one of those fields differs between two runs even when the package list is byte-for-byte identical. On a real SBOM with hundreds of components, the real change — one package added, one bumped — is a handful of lines lost inside dozens of metadata lines that changed for no reason you care about.

Is a structural diff ever the wrong choice?

Yes, when you need to audit the SBOM document itself rather than the packages it describes — checking that a required field like a license expression or a supplier name is present and correctly formatted on every component, or verifying the document's own metadata (spec version, tool provenance) for a compliance record. That is a document-validation task, not a change-detection task, and a raw JSON diff or a schema validator is the right tool for it.

Can I paste both files into an online JSON-diff tool instead?

You can, but an SBOM is a complete inventory of your build's dependencies, and for a proprietary product that inventory itself can be sensitive — internal package names, an unreleased component, or the sheer shape of your dependency tree. Uploading it to a third-party web tool just to answer "what changed" is a real information disclosure for a question that does not need one. This page reads both files in your browser and never sends them anywhere.

Does either approach tell me if a change is safe?

No. Neither a raw diff nor this tool's structural comparison says anything about whether an added or updated package is vulnerable, malicious, or appropriately licensed — both only show you that a change happened. Deciding whether the change is safe to ship is a separate step this tool does not do.

No warranty. This page and the linked tool apply a structural comparison to files you supply. They are provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied, and they are not a security audit or a compliance attestation. You are responsible for verifying anything here before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

This page names no specific product. "Diffing the raw JSON files" and "a generic online JSON-diff tool" describe a method and a category of tool, not any one company's product.

Nothing leaves your browser. The tool this page links to runs entirely client-side; nothing you paste is uploaded anywhere.

why-did-one-version-bump-show-up-as-doze.text:
← SBOM Diff Check

Why did bumping one package show up as dozens of changes?

You edited one line in package.json, requirements.txt, or go.mod, rebuilt, and the diff reports dozens of added, removed, and version-changed packages. That is usually the SBOM working correctly, not a sign anything went wrong — here is why the cascade happens and how to check it is the expected kind.

The SBOM records the whole install, not your one-line edit

syft, docker sbom, trivy, and cdxgen all walk the resolved dependency tree and record every package that actually ends up installed — direct and transitive alike. Bumping one direct dependency's version can change which versions its own dependencies resolve to, because most package managers re-resolve the whole tree rather than touching only the line you edited. A single version bump on a popular package can easily carry twenty or thirty transitive packages along with it, each showing up on this page as its own added, removed, or version-changed row.

This is not specific to this tool. A line-based diff of the raw SBOM JSON files would show the same cascade, just buried under the serial number and timestamp noise this tool already strips out — see how this compares to diffing the raw files by hand.

Telling an expected cascade from a real surprise

The question worth asking is not "how many rows changed" but "does every row trace back to the one thing I actually changed." Work it in this order:

  1. List what you actually edited — the one or few direct dependencies whose version constraint you changed.
  2. For each name the diff reports as added, removed, or version-changed, check whether it is a dependency (direct or transitive) of what you edited, using your package manager's own tree command (npm ls <pkg>, pip show <pkg>, go mod why <pkg>, or equivalent).
  3. If every row traces back to your edit, the cascade is expected — your lockfile or resolved tree changed exactly the way a dependency bump should.
  4. A row that has nothing to do with what you changed — a package your manifest never named and no changed dependency pulls in — is the one worth investigating: a stale lockfile committed by accident, a build environment that drifted, or a substitution attack are all things that would produce exactly that shape of finding.

Wiring --fail-on-change into CI without training people to ignore it

sbom_diff.py's --fail-on-change flag exits 2 the moment anything differs between the two SBOMs you give it — it does not distinguish an expected cascade from a real surprise, because it cannot see which dependency you meant to bump. Two shapes of pipeline get real value out of it, and one does not: 

python3 sbom_diff.py old.json new.json --fail-on-change  # exit 2 if anything differs
  • A build meant to be pinned or vendored, where no dependency change is ever expected between two runs — here a nonzero exit is exactly the signal you want, on every commit.
  • Not an ordinary pipeline that rebuilds after routine dependency bumps — there, this flag fails on the exact commits meant to change dependencies, and a gate that is red on purpose most of the time is a gate a team learns to re-run or override rather than read.

For the second shape, run without --fail-on-change and read the report as a diff to review, the same way you would read this page's table — not as a gate.

Common questions

Does this mean my dependency bump broke something?

Not by itself. A version-changed row means the resolved version differs between the two SBOMs, not that anything is broken — most of these rows are transitive packages whose version your package manager chose on your behalf when it re-resolved the tree, not lines you edited or reviewed.

How do I tell an expected cascade from a real supply-chain surprise?

Check whether every added, removed, or changed name is a dependency — direct or transitive — of the one package you bumped, using your package manager's own dependency-tree command. If every row traces back to that one edit, the cascade is expected. A name that has nothing to do with what you changed is the one worth investigating.

Should I wire --fail-on-change into my CI pipeline?

Only where no dependency change is ever expected, such as a build meant to be pinned or vendored. Wired into an ordinary CI pipeline that rebuilds after every dependency bump, --fail-on-change fails on the exact commits meant to change dependencies, which trains a team to ignore the gate rather than read it.

Why does the SBOM list packages I never installed directly?

Because syft, docker sbom, trivy, and cdxgen all record the full installed dependency tree, not just what your package.json, requirements.txt, or go.mod names directly. That is the SBOM doing its job — a build's actual attack surface is every package that ends up installed, not only the ones a human typed into a manifest.

Want the tool itself, or how it compares to the official CLI's own diff command? See SBOM Diff Check, or how this compares to cyclonedx-cli diff.
